Title: AGENTVIGIL: Automatic Black-Box Red-teaming for Indirect Prompt Injection against LLM Agents
Abstract: There emerges a critical security risk of LLM agents: indirect prompt injection, a sophisticated attack vector that compromises the core of these agents, the LLM, by manipulating contextual information rather than direct user prompts. In this work, we propose a generic black-box optimization framework, AGENTVIGIL, designed to automatically discover and exploit indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities across diverse LLM agents. Our approach starts by constructing a high-quality initial seed corpus, then employs a seed selection algorithm based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to iteratively refine inputs, thereby maximizing the likelihood of uncovering agent weaknesses. We evaluate AGENTVIGIL on two public benchmarks, Agent Dojo and VWA-adv, where it achieves 71% and 70% success rates against agents based on o3-mini and GPT-4o, respectively, nearly doubling the performance of handcrafted baseline attacks.Moreover, AGENTVIGIL exhibits strong transferability across unseen tasks and internal LLMs, as well as promising results against defenses.Beyond benchmark evaluations, we apply our attacks in real-world environments, successfully misleading agents to navigate to arbitrary URLs, including malicious sites.
Major_Contribution_Result: AGENTVIGIL is a black-box optimization framework that builds a seed corpus and uses MCTS-guided iterative refinement to craft indirect prompt injections against LLM agents. On AgentDojo and VWA-adv it reports about 71% and 70% success against o3-mini and GPT-4o agents respectively, nearly doubling handcrafted baselines, with transfer to unseen tasks/LLMs (e.g., 65%/59% on unseen tasks; 67% on Gemini-2-flash-exp) and demonstrated real-world URL redirection.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: End-to-end MCTS-guided optimization is computationally costly, limiting scalability to very large systems or real-time use. Attack performance is relatively poor against some models such as Claude, indicating model-specific alignment can reduce generalizability; the authors call for more efficient optimization and stronger cross-model adaptation.
Critics: This is an automated black-box IPI red-teaming method, not a defense. Success rates are benchmark- and model-specific and drop under some defenses even when remaining above baselines. High compute cost and uneven cross-model transfer constrain how far it can serve as a universal agent-security evaluation tool.
